To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the leader election problem and the degree recognition problem cannot be solved by any self-stabilizing protocols with global knowledge, (2) the ranking problem can be solved by self-stabilization protocols with global knowledge if the number of nodes is known, (3) the ranking problem and the degree-recognition problem can be solved if the number of edges is known, and (4) the neighbor recognition problem cannot be solvable by self-stabilizable population protocols with global knowledge.

(1) if we have the global knowledge of the number n of nodes in a graph, then we can solve all the above problems; (2) if we have only the global knowledge of m, the number of edges, then we can only solve the degree recognition problem; (3) if we have neither the knowledge of n nor the knowledge of m, then we can not solve any of the above problems.

(1) the leader election problem is not solvable by a self-stabilization protocol in arbitrary graphs if the knowledge of the number n of nodes in a graph is not available, and (2) the leader election, the ranking, the degree recognition, and the neighbor recog- nition problems are solvable by self-stabilization protocols in arbitrary graphs with the knowledge of the numbers n and e of nodes and edges, respectively.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the knowledge of the number n of nodes in a population protocol is enough to solve the leader election problem and the degree recognition problem in any network, and the knowledge of the numbers n and m of nodes and edges in a population protocol, respectively, is enough to solve any of the four problems in arbitrary graphs.
global knowledge can be used as a tool to design self-stabilizing protocols for some of the problems that cannot be solved without global knowledge.

the knowledge of the number $n$ of nodes in a graph is sufficient for the leader election, and the knowledge of the total number of edges in the graph is sufficient for solving the degree recognition and the neighbor recognition, and that these problems are unsolvable in a self-stabilezing way without the global knowledge.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the knowledge of the number n of nodes and the number m of edges in a graph can solve the problems of the leader election, the ranking, and the degree recognition in a self-stablizing manner in arbitrary graphs, while the knowledge of n alone can solve the neighbor recognition problem.
the number of nodes is a powerful global knowledge that enables us to design a wide variety of self-stabilization algorithms.

the knowledge of the number (or the size) of nodes is more useful in the sense that it allows us to design self-stabilizing protocols for all of the four problems, whereas the knowledge of the size of edges does not.
